examples.Factorial:
-- Tail-optimized factorial function using recursion.
let factorial x =
	 let rec fact_helper n acc =
		match n with
		| 0 = acc
		| _ = fact_helper (n - 1) (acc * n)
	in fact_helper x 1

 in factorial 5
examples.Fibonacci:
-- Tail-optimized Fibonacci function.
let fibonacci n =
	let rec fib_helper n a b =
		match n with
		| 0 = a
		| _ = fib_helper (n - 1) (a + b) a
	in fib_helper n 0 1

 in fibonacci 10
examples.List Sum:
-- Sum elements of a list using foldr.
let sum xs = foldr (+) 0 xs

in sum [1..5] -- Returns 15
examples.Filter Even:
-- Filter even numbers from a list.
let is_even x = x % 2 == 0
in filter is_even [1..10]
examples.Quick Sort:
-- Quick sort implementation using pattern matching.
let rec quicksort xs =
	match xs with
	| [] = []
	| pivot : tail =
		let less = filter (<= pivot) tail in
		let greater = filter (> pivot) tail in
		quicksort less ++ [pivot] ++ quicksort greater

in quicksort [3, 6, 8, 10, 1, 2, 1]

chapter_0_tutorial.name: Chapter 0 — Tutorial: Placing a Hex
chapter_0_tutorial.description:
[b]Welcome to Hexkell.[/b]

You build programs by placing hexagons, or [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img][b]hexes[/b] on a grid and wiring them together. The [b]Do[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex in the middle of every workspace is the program's main expression — whatever you wire into [b]Do[/b] is the answer the auditor checks.

Controls:

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/w.tres[/img][img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/a.tres[/img][img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/s.tres[/img][img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/d.tres[/img] to move the camera.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/mouse/middle_mb.tres[/img][img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/buttons/plus_icon.tres[/img][img valign=center, height=2em]res://assets/icons/input/mouse/all_directions.tres[/img] pans the camera and [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/mouse/scroll_wheel.tres[/img][b]wheel[/b] zooms.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/mouse/left_mb.tres[/img] places, opens and drags; [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/mouse/right_mb.tres[/img] cancels and closes.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/r.tres[/img] rotates whatever is on your cursor.

examples.name: Numbers
examples.caption: An [b]Int[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex wired into [b]Do[/b] — the simplest valid program.

chapter_1_integer_operators.name: Chapter 1 — Integer Operators
chapter_1_integer_operators.description:
Operator [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes combine wired inputs into a new value.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [code]+[/code] takes two wired inputs and emits their sum — its siblings ([code]- × ÷ %[/code]) unlock as you finish this chapter's work.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Wire two [b]Int[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes into the operator's input sides, then wire the operator into [b]Do[/b].
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Operators chain: the output of one can feed an input of the next.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Rotate a [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex ([img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/r.tres[/img]) to bring its input sides toward your wiring.

[color=#9fcfff]Tip:[/color] when the whole chain is made of literals and operators, the [b]Do[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex previews the computed value right on its body.

examples.name: Binary ops
examples.caption: Two [b]Int[/b] hexes feeding the NW + SW sides of a [b]+[/b] hex; the [b]+[/b]'s east output runs into [b]Do[/b].

chapter_2_boolean_literals.name: Chapter 2 — Boolean Literals
chapter_2_boolean_literals.description:
Not every answer is a number — some jobs ask for a verdict.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]true[/b] and [b]false[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes are output-only literals, just like [b]Int[/b].
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Wire one straight into [b]Do[/b] when the job expects a boolean.

[color=#9fcfff]Tip:[/color] the slide shows the boolean [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes as they appear in the editor.

examples.name: Booleans
examples.caption: [b]true[/b] / [b]false[/b] hexes; the comparison hexes ([code]==[/code], [code]<[/code], [code]>=[/code], [code]&&[/code]) take two inputs the same way [b]+[/b] does.

chapter_3_boolean_operators.name: Chapter 3 — Boolean Operators
chapter_3_boolean_operators.description:
Boolean operator [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes ask questions about wired values.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Comparisons — [code]== != < >=[/code] — take two numbers and emit [code]true[/code] or [code]false[/code].
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [code]&&[/code] and [code]||[/code] combine two booleans; [code]![/code] flips one.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] They wire exactly like the arithmetic operators: inputs in, verdict out — wire the comparison itself into [b]Do[/b] when a job asks for a judgement.

examples.name: Comparisons
examples.caption: [i]Screenshot pending — wire two values through a comparison hex and capture it with the top-bar Copy BP button.[/i]

chapter_4_identifiers.name: Chapter 4 — Identifiers & Names
chapter_4_identifiers.description:
Programs get powerful when values have names. First, learn to read the names a job hands you.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] The [b]id[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex references a name in scope. To the wiring it's just another value [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex — like an [b]Int[/b] whose number someone else fills in.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]Reserved identifiers[/b]: jobs hand you parameters as [code]white[/code] / [code]black[/code]. They appear in the [b]id[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex's picker only while that job is selected, and the client sets their values at submit time — that's why hard-coding the number fails.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Once you're comfortable reading identifiers, [b]Chapter 6 — Bindings[/b] shows how to name your own values with [b]let[/b], [b]let rec[/b], and [b]def[/b].

examples.name: Identifiers
examples.caption: An [b]id[/b] hex set to [b]white[/b] — the job exposes [code]white[/code] / [code]black[/code] as reserved parameters the auditor injects values into.

chapter_5_conditionals.name: Chapter 5 — Conditionals
chapter_5_conditionals.description:
Choose between two values with the [b]if[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]if[/b] takes its [b]condition[/b] on the outer face and answers with one of two values.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Wire a boolean (often a comparison from Chapter 3) into the condition side.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] Press [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/q.tres[/img] over it to descend and wire the [b]then[/b] / [b]else[/b] bodies inside — a move you'll reuse for [b]let[/b] and [b]match[/b].

Once finished with the inner body, you can press [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/e.tres[/img] to ascend.

examples.name: if
examples.caption: [b]if[/b] takes its condition on the outer face. Press [b]Q[/b] over it to descend and wire the [b]then[/b] / [b]else[/b] bodies inside — a shape you'll meet again in [b]let[/b] and [b]match[/b].

chapter_6_lambdas.name: Chapter 6 — Lambdas
chapter_6_lambdas.description:
[b]Lambdas[/b] ([code]λ[/code] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex) are anonymous functions written [code]\p1 p2 -> body[/code]. The [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex has 1–5 wired inputs (one per parameter); leaving any of them unwired produces a [b]partial application[/b] — a function value the next hex can apply further.

This chapter's job asks you to build a small one-parameter function — a [b]+1 machine[/b] the shop can apply to many crates.

examples.name: Lambdas
examples.caption: A [b]λ[/b] hex with one wired input is a one-parameter function. With zero inputs wired, the hex's output IS the function value itself — ready to be applied elsewhere.

chapter_7_bindings.name: Chapter 7 — Bindings
chapter_7_bindings.description:
Now that you can read names and stop with [b]if[/b], it's time to make your own bindings.

[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]let[/b] binds a wired value to a name; press [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/q.tres[/img]over it to descend into its body level.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]let rec[/b]'s bound name is also in scope inside its own value — that's what makes recursion possible. Always give it a base case (an [b]if[/b] that stops recursing) or it loops forever.
[color=#ffd86b]•[/color] [b]def[/b] floats at level 0 and broadcasts its name wirelessly into scope; multiple defs build a small library.

examples.name: let
examples.caption: [b]let[/b] binds a wired value to a name. Press [b]Q[/b] over the let hex to descend into its body level.

examples.name: let rec
examples.caption: [b]let rec[/b]'s bound name is also in scope inside its own value — needed for self-recursion (e.g. factorial).

examples.name: Definitions
examples.caption: [b]def[/b] floats at level 0 and broadcasts its name wirelessly into scope. Multiple [b]def[/b]s with the same name become multi-equation pattern matching.

chapter_8_structures.name: Chapter 8 — Structures
chapter_8_structures.description:
[b]Tuples[/b] are fixed-length "frozen" groups: [code](1, 2)[/code], [code](true, 0, 99)[/code]. You can't iterate them; you destructure with pattern matching to pull the parts out.

[b]Lists[/b] are variable-length sequences: [code][10, 20, 30][/code], [code][1..5][/code]. The cons operator [code]:[/code] prepends an element; [code]++[/code] concatenates two lists.

[b]Pattern matching[/b] on a list usually splits head + tail: [code]match xs with | [] = … | h:t = …[/code]. Pair it with recursion to walk the whole list.

The final chapter job asks you to rebuild [code]len[/code] or [code]map[/code] using pattern matching + recursion.

examples.name: Tuples
examples.caption: A [b]tuple[/b] hex — press [img valign=center, height=1.5em]res://assets/icons/input/keyboard/letters/q.tres[/img] to descend and wire its elements; emits [code](a, b)[/code].

examples.name: Lists
examples.caption: [b]list[/b] hex — elements live one level down; a full block can be descended into again for more. Nothing wired emits [code][][/code].

examples.name: : and ++
examples.caption: [b]:[/b] (cons) prepends a head; [b]++[/b] concatenates two lists end-to-end.

examples.name: Pattern match
examples.caption: [b]match[/b] hex with two branches — patterns [code][][/code] and [code]h:t[/code]. Press [b]Q[/b] to descend and wire each branch's body.

examples.name: Recursion on lists
examples.caption: A [b]def[/b] for [b]length[/b]: pattern-match on the input, recurse on the tail.

job_01_any_number.name: Pick a number
job_01_any_number.description: Wire an [b]Int[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex into the [b]Do[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex. The shop owner doesn't care which number — they just want to see the press run an end-to-end job.

job_02_add_crates.name: Add up the crates
job_02_add_crates.description: Two crates arrive: one holds [b]5[/b] parts, the other [b]3[/b]. Wire two [b]Int[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes into a [b]+[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex and run the total. The auditor wants to see the press do the sum — a pre-totalled [b]8[/b] gets rejected.

job_03_return_true.name: Print the all-clear
job_03_return_true.description: The shop floor wants a literal [b]true[/b] sign in the window. Place a [b]true[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex and wire it into [b]Do[/b]. Nothing else needed.

job_04_quality_check.name: Pass the quality check
job_04_quality_check.description: Quality control asks a simple question: is a [b]3[/b]-part crate lighter than a [b]5[/b]-part one? Wire the two numbers through a comparison [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex ([code]<[/code]) and let the press answer. A bare [b]true[/b] sign gets rejected — the auditor wants the comparison actually performed.

job_05_echo_white.name: Echo the shipment
job_05_echo_white.description: Today's job comes with a parameter: the client hands you [b]white[/b], an identifier already holding the crate count. Place an [b]id[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex, set it to [b]white[/b] in its config, and wire it straight into [b]Do[/b] — an identifier IS a value hex, no math needed. Typing the number yourself won't pass: the count changes with every shipment.

job_06_double_white.name: Double the shipment
job_06_double_white.description: The client hands you one parameter — [b]white[/b] — and wants its double. Wire an [b]Int[/b] literal, a [b]×[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex, and an [b]id[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex set to [b]white[/b]. The identifier picker will only enable [b]white[/b] while this job is selected.

job_07_compare_white_black.name: Is white smaller than black?
job_07_compare_white_black.description: Two parameters today: [b]white[/b] and [b]black[/b]. Return the truthfulness of [b]white[/b] being less than [b]black[/b] — i.e. wire a comparison [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex with two [b]id[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hexes feeding it. No fudging with a bare [b]true[/b] / [b]false[/b] literal: the auditor will reject programs that don't actually do the comparison.

job_08_pick_bigger.name: Pick the bigger of two crates
job_08_pick_bigger.description: Two parameters: [b]white[/b] and [b]black[/b]. Return whichever is larger. An [b]if[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex with a comparison from the last job is the most direct route — and the auditor checks that one was used.

job_09_increment_fn.name: Build a +1 machine
job_09_increment_fn.description: Return a function (a [b]λ[/b] [img valign=center, height=1em]res://assets/icons/hexagons/hollow_hex.tres[/img]hex with one parameter) that adds 1 to its input. The shop will apply it to several crates and check each one.

job_10_let_binding.name: Reuse the offset
job_10_let_binding.description: Bind an intermediate value once and reuse it: compute [code](white + 1)²[/code] by using a [b]let[/b] to name [code]white + 1[/code], then multiplying that name by itself. The auditor checks you used a [b]let[/b].

job_11_sum_list.name: Total the manifest
job_11_sum_list.description: Build a function that returns the sum of a list. The standard library exposes [code]foldr[/code], which collapses a list with a binary operator and a seed value.
